risk_flags.note: The firm may control key internal records and methodologies, making initial external judgments incomplete.
Potential internal witnesses may remain silent due to dependency on employer and fear of isolation.
Competitor amplification raises attention but may complicate public interpretation of the dispute's credibility.
City dependence on an active vendor may slow severe sanctions even if trust degrades.
A relatively small set of procurement actors may determine endpoint timing and framing.
Dueling frames of whistleblower credibility versus firm denial can harden before records are reviewed.

simulation_brief.summary: At T0, a fictional logistics software firm faces an allegation from an employee that delivery-time metrics were manipulated for a public contract. The firm publicly denies wrongdoing. A city procurement office has started a review. Drivers associated with service delivery report that the published metrics never matched operational reality. Competitors are amplifying the story. Terminal uncertainty centers on whether the review leads to audit escalation, temporary contract pause, exoneration, or contract termination.
simulation_brief.title: logistics metrics contract review
uncertainty_notes: Evidence quality is mixed at initialization; allegations, denials, driver testimony, and competitor amplification are all present but not yet adjudicated.
Decision authority appears partly concentrated in the city procurement office, with firm leadership controlling internal records and messaging.
Public controversy is active but not yet at maximum institutional crisis; multiple reversible process paths remain open.

sociology_baseline.note: Most actors update within existing trust boundaries; firm loyalists and critics interpret the same allegations differently.
Additional corroboration or documentary evidence could sharply increase willingness to speak.
Employment dependence and fear of isolation suppress open dissent inside the firm.
Actors cluster by institutional role and incentives, reinforcing shared interpretations.
Single allegation matters, but multiple corroborating sources are likely needed for major legitimacy shifts.
Organizational identity shapes defensive and accountability-oriented narratives.
Public attention may fade without new disclosures or formal action.

sociology_prompt_influences.description: City decision-makers face service continuity pressure, making immediate termination less automatic even under suspicion.
Employees with concerns may stay quiet due to career and retaliation risk.
Driver testimony can gain credibility when concrete operational mismatches are easy to describe.
Competitor involvement raises attention but can muddy perceived motive purity of the allegations.
Observers expect the procurement office to be neither captured by the vendor nor reckless about service disruption.
